banter.text: runs a thumb along a pew-back worn into two pale stripes.
"A hundred and forty years of hands. You can't buy that and you can't print it."
looks up at the steel plate on its much older bracket for a moment longer than the work requires.
stops in front of the photograph of a street that's still there and a skyline that's not.
"That corner is a bank now. The corner is fine. It's a good corner."

chitchat: replaces a candle on the rail, and squares the new one to the row.
wipes the brass on a fitting nobody has needed in forty years.
"The building is older than the congregation and the congregation is older than me. That order matters to somebody."
polishes the steel plate at the far end with a cloth kept for it, thoroughly, and without hurry.
"They come for the pantry, mostly. That's what a place like this is for, when it's working."
checks the boiler, listens to it, and writes something small in a notebook.
description: An old man in a cassock gone shiny at the elbows, with the build of somebody who was once much larger and the stillness of one who has learned it's usually enough. His hands are steady. He watches the door the way people who remember a different city watch doors, which is to say without appearing to.

options.label: You aren't going to name them.

aboutneil.text: "It's about several people," Father Jerome says, and doesn't name any of them.

before.text: "People want me to say it was better," he says. "It was not, mostly. It was cold and it was unfair and a great many people I liked died of things that are curable now." He puts the cloth down. "But I'll tell you one thing that was different, and you may do as you like with it. When something broke, a person came. Not a form. Not a queue. A person you could be angry at, who could be wrong, and who had to look at you."

options.label: That isn't much of a creed.

believe.text: "That's a larger question than you think you're asking," he says, "and I have watched what I say to it for a very long time, so you'll forgive a short answer." He sets the cloth down. "Something made all this and didn't stay to explain it. Everything after that's people trying to be decent without the instructions, and arguing about the wording." A shrug. "I was taught a particular wording. Most of the people who could argue it with me are dead. What's left is the decency, and I find that holds up better than the wording ever did."

options.label: And the plaque comes down on the Monday.

cameras.text: He considers that for slightly longer than a man would consider a question about screws. "They film on a Tuesday," he says.

options.label: Fourteen years is a long time to say them to nobody.

check.text: "Somebody reads a return, I expect," he says. "Nobody has ever come. In fourteen years nobody has come up that road to see whether an old man is saying the right words in an empty room." He shrugs, once. "I say them. They aren't hard to say."

options.label: That may be enough on its own.

comehere.text: "They do." He almost smiles. "Nobody is optimising this room. That may be all it is."

creed.text: "No," he agrees, pleasantly. "It fits on a card and it took me fifty years, which tells you something about the fifty years." He picks the cloth back up. "The long version is downstairs on a clipboard with a pen on a string."

evenknowing.text: "Especially then," he says. "A man who steals tinned beans out of a church is telling you something about his week, and I would rather be told." He squares the row of candles. "The clipboard isn't there to catch anybody. It's there so that when he's ready to talk about it, there's already a piece of paper with his handwriting on it and he doesn't have to start from the beginning."

eye.text: "It is," he says. "Compliance of Worship, ninth revision. The certificate is on my desk if you would like to see it, and it's in order." He looks up at the plate. "It was put in by a young man from the ward who did it properly and took two days over it. He drilled through a piece of carving to do it, and he apologised to me, and I told him he had done a good job. Both of those things were true."

options.label: You remember the old city, then.

howlong.text: "I was born at the turn of the century," he says, without any weight on it. "In the ward, not far. I have been in this building since I was a young man and I expect to be carried out of it." He straightens a candle. "It isn't a long time to a building. It's a long time to me."

options.label: Why do you let him stay?

neil.text: "He does." A long pause, and no complaint in it at all. "He's a rude, frightened, unwell man who's very funny about four times an hour, and he steals my supper, and he says things under my roof that I'll answer for." He puts the cloth down. "He also turns up. Every week, on time, in a building where nobody makes him. I have buried people who never managed that."

options.label: Somebody should have said it years ago.

notnothing.text: He stops what he's doing, briefly. "No," he says. "It isn't nothing. Thank you." And then he goes back to it.

nowadays.text: He considers the question for a while, which is itself an answer. "Now it's very efficient," he says. "I want to be fair. It's genuinely very efficient." He picks the cloth back up. "I'm old and I'm slow and I take up a great deal of room, and I have never once been efficient, and people still come up that road to sit in here. I have thought about why for about fifty years and I haven't got to the bottom of it."

options.label: Even knowing who takes from it?

pantry.text: "We do." He nods downward. "There's a sheet on a clipboard and a pen on a string and it works on the honour system, and I know precisely what you're about to ask me." He doesn't wait for it. "Yes. It's abused. It has always been abused. If I put a lock on that door I would keep out nine people who need it to keep out one who does not, and I have run that arithmetic every year since I was forty, and it has never once come out the other way."

options.label: It always seems to be down when the cameras are here.

plaque.text: "The fixing is poor," he says, without pausing what he's doing. "Four screws into a hundred-and-forty-year-old lintel. It works loose in the cold and it'll crack the stone if it's left to. So it comes down and it goes back up, and I keep the screwdriver on me." He squares the cloth on the shelf. "It's on the return as compliant and it's compliant. Anyone is welcome to come and look at it."

refused.text: "I could have," he agrees, mildly. "And there would be no pantry, and no boiler, and the building would be a fabrication shop by now with the pews sold on." He returns to the brass. "I'm not brave. I want that on the record, because people my age get given credit for a great deal of bravery they never showed. I'm here. That's the whole of what I have managed."

root.first: He looks up from the candle rail and takes you in without hurrying about it. "You're welcome here," he says. "That isn't a formula, though it has become one. Father Jerome. The pantry is downstairs and the door isn't locked."

That steel plate is newer than the bracket it's on.
You take the plaque down sometimes.
You feed people out of that pantry.
Neil McManistan films in your basement.

root.text: "You're welcome here," he says, and goes on with what he was doing.

text_by_relation.familiar: "Sit down before you ask me anything," he says, "you have a face on you," and puts the cloth down.
text_by_relation.known: "Back again." He doesn't stop working. "There's tea in the vestry, and it isn't good tea."

throwout.text: "And he would go where?" he asks. It isn't rhetorical; he waits, and there's no answer, and he accepts that. "Quite," he says.

options.label: Then I hope you're right about him.

whystay.text: "Because he isn't finished," he says. "That isn't a sentiment, it's an observation, and I have made it about a great many people and been wrong perhaps a third of the time." He glances at the stairs down to the kitchen. "A man who was finished wouldn't bother being angry. The anger is the part I'm hopeful about."

goes and stands where he can see the road, without making anything of it.

after: Father Jerome comes back out with the plaque and sets it over the lower line of the carving.
Father Jerome drives the four screws home and checks with a thumb that it sits square.
Father Jerome goes back in. The building is compliant, and says so.
before: Father Jerome comes out with a short screwdriver and looks up at the lintel for a moment.
Father Jerome backs out four screws, one at a time, and lifts the steel plaque down off the stone.
Father Jerome stands there with the plaque in both hands, reading the line underneath it.
Father Jerome carries the plaque inside under one arm, the way you carry a tray.
